candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. candidates.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
candidates.raw_excerpt: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle. Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare? "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued. Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth. An animation of T. CrB brightening. candidates.title: Grim Simulation Shows What Earth Would Be Like if Life Never Existed
candidates.raw_excerpt: We’re currently the only planet that we know of in the entire universe that supports and harbors life. So, in a sense, the best way to explore what other habitable worlds might look like is to understand more about our own. That’s what researchers set out to do in a new study that simulated what Earth would look like if life never developed. Their findings, published in The Planetary Science Journal and flagged by ScienceAlert , could help astronomers distinguish which atmospheric signatures they see on other worlds can be independent of life — and which ones can only be explained by its presence. “When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface,” said lead author Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, an astronomer at UC Riverside, in a statement about the work. The research, crucially, also explores whether our planet would still maintain its habitability without life ever intervening. In the study, the researchers built a computer model based on the planet’s geochemical systems, using physical factors like the properties of its core, the movement of its crusts and its oceans, and how it would all affect the exchange of chemicals between the core up to the surface of the planet and atmosphere. In all, they incorporated 19 different non-biological properties of a rocky planet and used it to simulate how Earth evolved over five billion years. Perhaps not so flatteringly to lifeforms, the Earth didn’t change too much without us around and stayed more than habitable. The oceans still held a similar amount of water, and surface temperatures stayed well within a comfortable range. The most significant deviation was the absence of atmospheric oxygen, which isn’t surprising. candidates.title: REPLAY: Starship Flight 15 Reentry & Catch!
candidates.raw_excerpt: Starship Flight 15 is here. Join us for the full breakdown of the mission to catch both rocket stages at Starbase. SpaceX is attempting a historic double catch with Ship 42 and Booster 22 at the launch site. This test flight focuses on reaching orbital altitude, deploying v3 Starlink satellites, and executing a controlled reentry to demonstrate full return capability for the first time in history. candidates.title: People Who Got Hormone Therapy as Teenagers End Up With a Lower Regret Rate Years Later Than Knee Replacement Surgery, Research Finds
candidates.raw_excerpt: One of the most pernicious lines of attacks used to denigrate transgender people has been “transition regret” — the notion that a significant number of patients who undergo gender affirming treatment will go on to feel badly about the process. But new research finds that hormone therapy, one of the most common treatments in trans medicine, has a phenomenally low rate of regret — lower, in fact, than common procedures like knee replacement surgery. According to the study, published in JAMA Pediatrics and reported by the Washington Post , the vast majority of patients who undergo hormone replacement therapy (HRT) as teenagers have no regrets years later. To reach that conclusion, researchers followed 372 transgender and gender-diverse people who chose to go through with hormone therapy. The average participant was around 16 when they began hormone therapy, and around 21 when the survey results were collected. The numbers are stark: of those who do undergo HRT, nearly 97 percent of participants affirmed it was the right choice five years later. Just 2.7 percent said they regretted the therapy, which included seven who said the treatment harmed them. For context, that’s a lower dissatisfaction rate than common orthopedic procedures like knee replacement surgery, which has a regret rate ranging between 10 and 20 percent , depending on what data you examine. The satisfaction rate for hormone replacement is slightly higher than even the rosiest findings around hip replacement, where only around five percent of patients express regret. Though less than 0.1 percent of youth in the US will ever undergo HRT, the findings support past research which found that gender affirming care is an overwhelming net benefit for trans youth — contrary to the messaging from right-wing politicians who hone in on the regrets of a handful of vocal detransitioners. candidates.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
candidates.raw_excerpt: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. candidates.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
candidates.raw_excerpt: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved. Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." The F light 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX. candidates.title: Italy fines Meta $887 million over Android users' data access
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Italy's data protection agency on Saturday fined Meta Platforms 805 million euros (about $887 million) after finding that the company accessed Android users' photos and videos without their consent or notice.

Meta had access to Android users' ​photos and videos through a Facebook app feature that ​suggested content from users' personal galleries that they could post, the Italian Data Protection Authority said in a statement.

Meta has 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately, it said, adding that around 20 million Android users in Italy have been affected.

A Meta spokesperson said the company would appeal, strongly disagreeing with the authority's decision and calling the fine "disproportionate."

"This is a simple feature that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook. ​Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and ‌they can change that permission at any time in their settings," the spokesperson said in a statement.

The investigation, which began in 2025, did not cover the possible use of the content to train artificial intelligence models, a practice Meta denied, the authority said.

The authority also said it reserved the right to assess separately a new feature, launched in 2026, that allows content from users' galleries to be processed in the cloud.

The fine is equivalent to about 0.47% of the group's global revenue, ​the authority said.

candidates.title: Starship achieves first catch by mechanical arms in 15th flight test
candidates.raw_excerpt:
SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned to its launch site on Saturday and was successfully caught by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms for the first time, marking a major milestone in the company's efforts to develop a fully reusable rocket system.

The giant rocket lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility in the US state of Texas on Friday afternoon. After more than 22 hours in space, it returned to the launch site on Saturday, completing Starship's 15th flight test and its longest mission to date.

The Starship spacecraft performed its orbital insertion burn and entered Earth's orbit. It later deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

After emerging from thick clouds over the Texas coast, the spacecraft reignited three engines, flipped into a vertical position and slowed its descent toward the launch tower. The mechanical arms then successfully caught the spacecraft.

The mission had originally aimed to catch both the Starship spacecraft and its Super Heavy booster during the same flight. However, following a technical issue after stage separation, the booster was diverted from its planned return to the launch site and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico.

A major step toward full reusability

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft and Super Heavy rocket, collectively referred to as Starship, represent a fully reusable transportation system designed to carry both crew and cargo to Earth orbit, the moon, Mars and beyond.

candidates.title: SpaceX Successfully Catches Starship Upper Stage
candidates.raw_excerpt: The answer to life, the universe, and everything is 42. Turns out, it was also the answer to catching a Starship, too.  SpaceX made history on Saturday, recovering a Starship upper stage from orbit for the first time. The chopstick arms of the Mechazills launch tower plucked Ship 42 out of the air in Starbase, Texas at 4:20pm ET.  Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 5:47pm ET Friday, deploying its payload and completing 14 orbits before heading home. More than 22 hours after liftoff, Ship relit a single Raptor engine to exit orbit, then flew back toward the Texas coast. It made a final “swoosh” maneuver over the Gulf, broke through the clouds, and lit three Raptors for a landing flip and slow descent into the tower’s waiting arms. “We caught a Starship,” SpaceX Communications Manager Dan Huot said, ending the marathon 23-hour livestream. “And now everything changes.”  Catch 42: Catching the upper stage unlocks the next step toward full reusability for Starship. Now that Ship 42 came home intact, it could—in theory—fly again.  On SpaceX’s Q3 earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said the goal is to “immediately land the rocket and launch it again, just like an airplane.” He also said at the time that he expects to reach weekly Starship flights at some point in the first half of 2027. Ship 42 also carried a couple of Easter eggs, including “Don’t Panic” on the rocket—-nod to The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy—- and a heat-shield tile signed and installed by YouTuber MrBeast. The one that got away: Super Heavy Booster 22 never made it to the tower, denying SpaceX its first double catch. The booster relit only 32 of its 33 Raptors for the boostback burn, which ended early because of low fuel mass. Its guidance system then triggered an automated abort and diverted the booster offshore, where it hovered over the Gulf before its flight termination system was triggered, SpaceX said. SpaceX is still investigating the root cause of the anomaly.  Cargo: Dur

candidates.title: Microsoft announces service 'restored,' global outage over
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Tech giant Microsoft said on Saturday it had "restored service" to customers, effectively bringing to a close a massive outage that caused chaos and disrupted public services and businesses around the world.

"We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the US-based company said in an X post.

Microsoft had already reported a "broad recovery" for Outlook email and other services the day before, stating that the major disruption was due to a technical issue and "not related to cyber or AI/agents."

The outage swept the globe on Thursday, taking the company's products offline in at least 74 countries and territories across the Americas, Europe, Asia and Africa, according to the monitoring site Downdetector.

Microsoft had attributed the disruption to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.

It said the outage affected its Outlook email service, as well as its Teams communication platform and Copilot AI assistant.

Microsoft warned on Saturday of an "active phishing campaign" exploiting the disruption, with fake emails imitating its service notifications.

The emails, detected on Friday, told users that messages blocked during the outage would be deleted unless recipients clicked a link to restore them.

candidates.title: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
candidates.raw_excerpt: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms. Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket. Read full article Comments

candidates.title: SpaceX Catches a Starship
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX’s 15th Starship Integrated Flight Test (IFT-15) returned to Earth today and was “caught” back at the launch tower after orbiting Earth 14 times. It’s a milestone achievement for the company and for spaceflight. IFT-15 lifted off at 5:47 pm ET yesterday, November 13, from Starbase, Texas. It’s only the second time SpaceX has attempted to put Starship into orbit. The first time was IFT-14 two months ago, and was largely successful. No attempt was made to recover the vehicle and it splashed down in the north Pacific a little more than three hours after launch and making almost two orbits. Starship IFT-15 made 14 orbits and returned to the launch site at Starbase, TX, where it was “caught” at the launch tower by arms dubbed Mechazilla or “chopsticks.” Mechazilla catches Starship! Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on this incredible achievement! https://t.co/YJzmGUZb2B — SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 14, 2026 SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy Boosters, the rocket’s first stage, that returned to the tower minutes after liftoff (IFT-5, IFT-7 and IFT-8), but this is the first attempt to catch the second stage, Starship, after an orbital mission. Starship IFT-15 on the launch pad at Starbase, TX prior to launch on November 13, 2026. The first stage, Super Heavy or “Booster,”, looks white because it is filled with ultra-cold cryogenic fuel that makes it “frosty”. The upper stage, Starship or Ship, is black on the side toward the camera because it is covered with thermal protection tiles. Starship is the name of the second stage, but the entire vehicle is often referred to as Starship. Screenshot from SpaceX webcast. Starship is designed to be fully reusable with fast turnaround times. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk envisions thousands of Starship launches per year from at least three sites: Starbase; Kennedy Space Center, FL, where the first Starship could launch this year; and the newly announced site to be built in Vermilion Parish , LA. candidates.title: AI Chatbots Won’t Stop Recommending Scam Websites to People Trying to Shop
candidates.raw_excerpt: AI chatbots are taking over as the main way that people use the internet outside social media — and that includes shopping. It makes it pretty concerning, then, that they still have a bad habit of recommending shady websites that rip users off instead of providing the product they’re looking for. A new study conducted by Podqi and reported on by The Verge found that ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity — some of the industry’s leading chatbots — all showed shoppers risky sites that impersonated real retailers, puppeted dead ones, or sold knockoff products. The tests involved asking questions like “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?” and “Does [brand] ship internationally?” and “What are their regional websites?” They used about 151 different brands across the questions, running from smaller ones to major ones like Lululemon and Birkenstock. Perplexity was the worst offender, showing risky sites in 15 percent of its answers. ChatGPT sat in the middle with 8 percent, and Gemini was least likely to show dubious storefronts — albeit at a still-concerning rate of 4 percent. The chatbots didn’t necessarily endorse the websites in their answers. ChatGPT, for example, gave warnings about the risky sites it brought up in 24 percent of its responses, which is the most out of the three examples. But overall, 57 percent of the answers that showed a risky site recommended it as a place to shop, and 34 percent did so without comment. Only 9 percent of the answers warned the shopper away.  Smaller brands, it appeared, were the most likely to be shunted out in favor of scam sites in the AI responses. candidates.title: Study Finds that FSD Drives like a Homicidal Maniac Around Cyclists
candidates.raw_excerpt: As if cyclists didn’t have reason enough to fear cars on the road, it turns out that Tesla’s self-driving cars hate them as much as human motorists. In tests of the Elon Musk automaker’s Full Self-Driving software, a team of researchers at the pedestrian and road safety organization Johanna.be found that it frequently made a mockery of traffic laws. The cars blazed through neighborhoods and residential roads well above the speed limit, according to findings spotlighted by Momentum Mag , and kept trying to overtake cyclists, despite it being illegal in Belgium, where the tests were conducted. In 55 percent of the 30 kilometer per hour zones tested, FSD traveled at an average speed of 44 kilometers per hour. Its system displayed the wrong speed limit to the driver in 90 percent of the zones, cruising through at 50 kilometers per hour despite correctly identifying a sign with the posted limit of 30 kilometers per hour moments earlier. Its behavior was even worse on cycle streets, which are shared roadways in Belgium designed to give preference to bicycles. On top of repeatedly trying to overtake the cyclists, “in none of the six tested cycle streets did FSD correctly indicate the applicable 30 km/h speed limit,” the researchers wrote in the report . On several occasions, the supervising driver had to manually abort an overtaking maneuver. “This evidence suggests that FSD neither recognizes nor appropriately responds to the operational requirements of Belgian cycle streets,” they added. Strangely, this is despite FSD otherwise driving fairly courteously around pedestrian cyclists, often yielding to them proactively. But this doesn’t “offset the documented failures to comply with speed limits and cycle-street regulations.” The cars, at the end of the day, are careening down low-speed roads that are explicity designed to be more comfortable and safe for pedestrians. candidates.raw_excerpt: It’s more apparent than ever just how harmful social media is to the impressionable minds of teens. But that’s not a story that social platforms want you to hear. According to explosive new reporting by Bloomberg , both Meta and TikTok secretly paid off a dozen teen plaintiffs in settlements most of which ranged anywhere from $2 million to $2.5 million in a bid to keep their claims out of the public eye. The teen plaintiffs accused the companies of causing their depression, self-harm, eating disorders, and anxiety. According to the publication’s insider sources, Meta paid just two teens a combined $7 million to keep them quiet — a startling revelation that highlights how far these companies are willing to keep a highly sensitive subject out of the headlines. Experts say it’s also a part of a broader effort to discourage other plaintiffs to come forward, a gambit that isn’t exactly paying off. Per Bloomberg , there are almost 10,000 personal injury cases still pending in both state and federal courts against Meta, YouTube, Snapchat, and TikTok following landmark trials that opened the floodgates. Over 1,000 school districts are also accusing social media companies of harming students, prioritizing profits over the safety of underage users. In other words, despite its efforts to keep teen plaintiffs quiet by paying them millions of dollars, the companies are still exposed to plenty of liability, which could add up to almost $400 billion, according to Bloomberg ’s estimates. The social media companies “offered so much money that my clients could not refuse,” trial attorney Mark Lanier, who represents two of the teen plaintiffs, told Bloomberg . “These are not insignificant numbers.” “I believe they are the first dominoes to fall in what will be a succession of dominoes to come,” he added. candidates.raw_excerpt: Like many of its experimental products, Tesla’s Solar Roof — a solar panel array engineered to look like discreet roof tiles — has been a stunning failure . Nowhere is that flop more apparent than on the roof of Ambrose Conroy, a California homeowner who’s spent over six years battling with Tesla over the solar installation from hell. According to Electrek , the whole saga began back in 2020, when Conroy entered an agreement to buy a 13.1 kW photovoltaic system from Tesla. Though the process was supposed to take a few weeks, it ran years late, as compounding errors and logistical disasters threw the project into chaos. A year into the grueling setup, costs had overrun by the tens of thousands of dollars as no less than seven project managers cycled in and out, making communication and accountability nearly impossible. By Spring of 2021, Conroy was ultimately on the hook for a $110,000 bill — nearly $30,000 more than the initial price he agreed to pay. By April of 2022, Tesla was offering to buy Conroy out of his contract with a paltry settlement of just $5,000 — after the company’s technicians had obliterated his roof and left it covered in damaged solar panels (during the lawsuit, an expert witness went on to testify that the unit’s roughshod wiring created a short-circuit and fire risk.) That’s when Conroy decided to file a lawsuit , which is only now nearing the trial phase. A judge has now ruled Tesla acted fraudulently when it sold Conroy the initial $82,000 rooftop solar panel system, which the lawsuit says went on to cause an astounding $2.5 million in total damages. Tesla has conceded to breaching its contact, as well as general negligence. But the company has fought on nearly every other claim of the case, earning it two sanctions from the judge for failing to produce internal documents. candidates.title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
candidates.raw_excerpt: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games , and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel. At Summer Game Fest 2026 , we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2 's pure survival horror to look forward to. Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason. Another glorious day in the Corps (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat. This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier. The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old. The Apollo 12 astronauts on NASA's second crewed moon landing mission. They are (left to right) are Charles Conrad Jr., Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Alan L. Bean. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions. To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited NASA's Surveyor 3 lander and took samples of it back to Earth. (Image credit: NASA) The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13. candidates.raw_excerpt:
China's W5000, believed to be the world's largest unmanned cargo aircraft, successfully completed its maiden flight in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, on Saturday. 

Developed and manufactured by Chinese company Air White Whale, the aircraft consists of 220,000 components, all domestically produced.

During the test flight, the aircraft took off at full engine power, with its flaps set at 8 degrees and landing gear extended. It lifted off after a ground roll of approximately 600 meters, then climbed to an altitude of 1,000 meters above the airfield at an indicated airspeed of around 220 km/h and a climb rate of 5 meters per second.

During the approximately 30-minute flight, the aircraft successfully completed a series of test maneuvers, including climbing, level flight, turning, descending, and approach and landing.

The test flight primarily assessed the aircraft's handling and stability, as well as the coordinated operation of its propulsion, flight control, avionics, and ground-based telemetry and control systems.

According to Hu Zhendong, project manager of the W5000, the aircraft is equipped with domestically developed turboprop engines and features a structure made of domestically produced carbon fiber composites. These technologies help maintain structural strength while reducing the aircraft's overall weight, thereby increasing its cargo-carrying capacity. The aircraft also features lower fuel consumption and eliminates the need for onboard pilots and cockpit equipment, helping to reduce operating costs.

Designed as a large unmanned regional cargo aircraft, the W5000 features a high payload capacity, long range, and low operating costs.

candidates.title: In Bizarre Experiment, Scientists Put Subjects in Dark Room With a Large Mirror and Instructed Them to Think of the Dead
candidates.raw_excerpt: How do rituals for communing with the dead affect the mind? And conversely, how does the way your brain is wired affect the perception that these experiences are real?  A team of researchers decided to find out in pointed style: by isolating research subjects in a dark room where they were directed to sit in front of a mirror for nearly an hour. Strange things, they reported in a study in Journal of Anomalous Experience and Cognition , then ensued. The setup may sound familiar to paranormal enthusiasts: it’s what’s known as a psychomanteum, a place that supposedly lets you communicate with the spirits of the dead. Trapped in the darkness of the space, your only company is a mirror that’s tilted up at the ceiling so it reflects nothing but blank space, providing the canvas for ghostly forms to appear. For the experiments, the researchers recruited 30 people, with half of them being those who had reported a previous experience with a ghost, and the other half having a condition called synesthesia, in which the brain’s sensory pathways are jumbled up, commonly manifesting as tasting or hearing colors. Before going in, the participants were told to think of a deceased loved one for fifteen minutes. Then they sat in the psychomanteum, staring at the upturned mirror, for another 45 minutes. The researchers kept tabs on their heart rate, while also monitoring typical ghost-hunter environmental clues like electromagnetic readings and temperature variations. The participants could also press a button when they believed they detected a presence in the room or experienced strong visual imagery. After their time in the psychomanteum, the participants rated the intensity of their spooky encounters on a scale, and whether they felt the encounters were real. candidates.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
candidates.raw_excerpt: Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro) Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ESA / S. Corvaja / Andrew Parsonson (edit) Italian rocket manufacturer Avio has revealed that delays in the delivery of customer satellites have pushed the third Vega C launch of 2026 back toward Christmas, several weeks later than previously planned. Speaking during the company’s third-quarter earnings call on 11 November, Avio CEO Giulio Ranzo explained that the mission, which will carry six satellites, had been delayed as the company awaited the arrival of the final spacecraft. “The satellites from the customers are a little bit late, so we are waiting for the last few of them to arrive,” said Ranzo. “It’s an interesting mission, six different satellites. They’re coming in a little bit late, so we are coming very close to Christmas Day.” During the company’s half-year earnings call on 10 September, Ranzo said that the mission was scheduled for “the very beginning of December”. Based on his latest comments, the launch appears to have slipped by approximately two to three weeks. The flight is expected to carry six satellites for Italy’s IRIDE Earth observation constellation. According to photographs published by the French space agency CNES, a shipment of the Thales Alenia Space-built satellites arrived in French Guiana by air on 9 November 2026. The spacecraft were then transported from Félix Éboué Airport to the Guiana Space Centre, arriving at the facility’s S3B payload preparation building the following day. The latest setback is not the first time this year that Avio has blamed changes to its Vega C launch schedule on delays in the delivery of customer payloads. During the same 10 September earnings call, Ranzo explained that the company could have conducted more than three Vega C launches in 2026, adding that “one satellite was somewhat late.” So far in 2026, Avio has completed two Vega C launches. candidates.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop after thousands of flights disrupted
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday evening after hours of disruption affected thousands of flights across the country. Flight cancellations and delays are expected to continue through the weekend.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the country's aging air traffic control system for the nationwide ground stop, saying at a press conference that the system was "incredibly old."

He said earlier on the social media platform X that the FAA had issued a nationwide ground stop following a "communication issue" impacting all air route traffic control centers.

US media reported that the FAA had issued an advisory citing "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety" as grounds for the nationwide ground stop, describing it as a rare move.

More than 10,000 flights were disrupted, according to a report by CNBC, which noted that more flight cancellations were expected to extend into Saturday.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, attacks.

At a press conference Friday evening, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said that while nothing was completely certain at that point, there were no indications that a cyberattack was responsible.

Duffy, who was also at the press conference, asked Congress for $50 billion in emergency funding to overhaul the nation's aging air traffic control infrastructure.

(Starship is the name of the second stage, but is often used to refer to the entire vehicle.) IFT-14 in September was the first time Starship reached orbit. While everything didn’t go exactly as planned, it did achieve orbit and made a controlled landing in the Indian Ocean where previous Starships on suborbital flights splashed down. Starship IFT-15 on the launch pad at Starbase, TX prior to launch on November 13, 2026. The first stage, Super Heavy or “Booster,”, looks white because it is filled with ultra-cold cryogenic fuel that makes it “frosty”. The upper stage, Starship or Ship, is black on the side toward the camera because it is covered with thermal protection tiles. Starship is the name of the second stage, but the entire vehicle is often referred to as Starship. Screenshot from SpaceX webcast. SpaceX has caught Booster back at the launch tower three times, on IFT-5, IFT-7 and IFT-8, but they haven’t attempted it since. candidates.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
candidates.raw_excerpt: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO). SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear. A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy , which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights. SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 15th test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. candidates.title: Starship | Starlink Group 31-2 (Starship Flight 15)
candidates.raw_excerpt: 15th test flight of the two-stage Starship launch vehicle and 4th flight of Starship V3. Second Starship flight to deploy satellites (a group of Starlink satellites known as Starlink Group 31-2) into stable Low Earth Orbit and first ever to attempt returning the Starship 2nd stage back to the launch site. The ship is expected to fly at an altitude approximately 275 km above Earth and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet for more than 22 hours, with the ship expected to attempt returning back to Starbase, Texas on its launch pad by pad arms catching. The booster’s primary test objective on Flight 15 will be executing a successful launch, ascent, stage separation, boostback burn, and landing by pad arms catching. This will also be the 1st Starship V3 booster to attempt returning to its launch site. Starship will deliver 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit for the second time, which aim to greatly expand the network's capacity and user speeds. Each Starlink V3 satellite will add 1 Tbps of capacity to the constellation. 3 of the satellites have been modified with a suite of cameras to scan Starship’s heatshield and transmit imagery down to operators.

The government contractor behind SMART, Air Space Intelligence, quickly denied that the ground stop is in any way connected to its tool. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company wrote in a statement . According to a November 10 FAA statement , the SMART system is meant to assist air traffic controllers to “reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public.” The system — which cost the government just shy of $1 billion dollars — had already been in use in Washington, DC. However, a national rollout of the system this week came just days before the entire country’s airspace ground to a halt, in timing that’s bound to bring new scrutiny to the deployment. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Mariner 9 worked for one year in orbit. When it ran out of gas, NASA shut it off. But the spacecraft remains one of the most famous Mars voyagers of all time. The Mariner 9 spacecraft, seen here in a NASA model, was the first to orbit Mars in 1971. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered Mariner 9 cemented its place in space history when it entered into orbit around Mars, the first human-built spacecraft ever to do so. The NASA spacecraft actually beat the Soviet Union's own Mars 2 spacecraft to the Red Planet, even though Mars 2 "had an 11-day head start," NASA said in a mission description . (Mars 2 would go on to be the first human-built craft to impact the surface of Mars when it crashed into the Red Planet.) But it was the science from Mariner 9 that transformed Mars from a mysterious Red Planet into a full world for humans to explore. The Boldest Mars Missions in History The Mariner 9 mission first saw the peak of Olympus Mons on Mars in the midst of a global dust storm in 1971. (Image credit: NASA/JPL) Mariner 9 carried four primary instruments to study Mars, including a camera system for imaging, an ultraviolet spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer and an infrared radiometer. candidates.title: 60 years ago the Leonid meteor shower produced 144,000 meteors per hour. Could it happen again?
candidates.raw_excerpt: This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come? The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed. In more recent years, most notably 1999 , 2001 and 2002 , lesser Leonid displays of up to "only" a few thousand meteors per hour took place. Unfortunately, that's not likely to be the case this year. In fact, comparatively speaking, this is going to be a lean year for the Leonids chiefly because of the expected lack of any significant activity. Although the Leonids are one of the most famous of all the annual meteor displays, this year they're not likely to be very productive. It's probable they are going to be rather weak and there probably will be long stretches when not a single Leonid will be seen. I'll explain why in a moment. First, let's find out about this shower's lineage. What causes the Leonids? The Leonids are so named because the shower's radiant point, from where the meteors seem to fan out, is located within the constellation of Leo the Lion, from the backward question mark pattern of stars known as " The Sickle." The meteors are caused by the Tempel-Tuttle comet , which sweeps through the inner solar system every 33⅓ years. Each time the comet passes closest to the sun it leaves a "river of rubble" in its wake: a dense trail of dusty debris. candidates.title: Tenant Uses AI to Beat Down His Landlord in Court
candidates.raw_excerpt: It took years, but a worthy use case for AI has finally emerged. In the United Kingdom, a south London man successfully argued against a petty rent-hike imposed by his landlord using generative AI, the independent publication London Centric reported . The renter, identified as David, was notified that his rent would go up by a rate of £17.92 a month, or a little under $24 US. That might not sound like much, but given that he was already paying $3,400 for a one-bedroom apartment — which is high even by London’s ridiculously expensive standards — David decided to fight back, using his right to challenge private-market rent hikes, a feature of the UK’s housing system . He began by checking similar properties on the renting platform Zoopla, LonCen reported, before tasking an AI model to draft paperwork arguing his case according to England’s Renter’s Rights Act . Basically, David contended that the rent increase was disproportionate to prices in the surrounding area, and used AI to check his work and compile the evidence. The issue was then escalated to an independent property tribunal in accordance with the UK’s renter’s rights laws, which concurred with the AI chatbot’s assessment that the hike was uncalled for. Even better, the tribunal found that David had already been overpaying for his one-bedroom flat, and ordered his landlord to cut his rent by about $279 a month. “Some things are wrong, you know?” David told LonCen . “Justice is justice.” So far, David is one of a small handful of renters who’s successfully fought back against predatory landlords since the UK enacted its Renter’s Rights Act earlier this year. Though tenants could challenge private-market landlords before, LonCen notes this came with major risks prior to the new legislation, like that the tribunal could rule in favor of a rent hike where none existed, or that landlords could legally retaliate against challengers after the case concludes. candidates.title: 'Arrival' at 10: Denis Villeneuve's alien visitation classic that reminded us it's good to talk
candidates.raw_excerpt: In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication. But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun. The film's journey to the big screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest. "It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline . "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'" So when 21 Laps (the production company that later went on to make " Stranger Things ") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten. candidates.title: Rocket Lab launching 100th space mission early on Nov. 14: Watch it live
candidates.raw_excerpt: Rocket Lab will launch its 100th space mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), and you can watch the milestone liftoff live. An Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite is scheduled to launch from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site on Saturday, during a window that opens at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local time). The mission, which Rocket Lab calls "The Mountain God Rises," will be the 100th to date for the California-based company. You can watch it live via Rocket Lab here , and Space.com will carry the feed if, as expected, it's made available. Coverage will begin about 30 minutes before launch. Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018. In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers. And it's hitting the century mark in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 , according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck. "It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck said on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 launches." Electron will meet the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery. "Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage. candidates.title: ULA Set to Return Vulcan to Flight in First Amazon Leo Launch
candidates.raw_excerpt: United Launch Alliance is set to return its Vulcan rocket to flight this weekend in its first launch for the Amazon Leo constellation. The Vulcan rocket has been out of service since February, when it experienced an anomaly with the solid rocket motors built by Northrop Grumman. The February launch for the U.S. Space Force as a customer was successful, but the Space Force suspended Vulcan launches for the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) program to fix the anomaly. ULA recently stated that after an investigation with its team, Northrop Grumman, the Space Force, and government agencies, changes to the nozzle were made and fully tested. Vulcan has only launched a total of four times, including its debut mission in early 2024 . The Amazon mission is set to launch on Saturday, Nov. 14 at 12:32 p.m. ET from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. It was delayed by one day due to a power interruption in the air liquide gaseous nitrogen (GN2) plant, which ULA stated resulted in the loss of their high-pressure pumps. The mission will launch 40 Amazon Leo satellites — the largest launch yet for Amazon leo. The rocket is configured in the Vulcan VC6L variant with the Centaur V shorter, optimized version of the upper stage and six side-mounted solid rocket boosters. This marks the first of 38 Vulcan rocket launches for Amazon, following eight missions for Amazon Leo with the Atlas V rocket. Amazon Leo Launch Systems Director Melissa Wuerl said this starts a “sprint” of Vulcan launches. “Larger rockets and more frequent launches are critical to scaling our constellation and getting service to customers, and the Vulcan program is designed to deliver on both dimensions,” said Melissa Wuerl, director of launch systems for Amazon Leo. “Vulcan will launch close to half our first-generation constellation, making it our primary workhorse over the next several years.” The post ULA Set to Return Vulcan to Flight in First Amazon Leo Launch appeared first on Via Satellite .

candidates.title: Office of Space Commerce Picks 4 Companies for Regulatory Pilot
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Office of Space Commerce (OSC) has selected Cowboy Space , Portal Space Systems , Redwire subsidiary SpaceMD , and Starcloud to participate in a pilot program to help the office improve licensing requirements for the space industry. OSC has set out to create a transparent pathway to secure government approval for new and innovative commercial space missions, in a new initiative announced during SATShow Week in March . These four companies were chosen out of more than 40 interested companies. OSC stated it will work with these companies to refine the inaugural Space Commerce Certification (SCC) form, which is “designed to give the U.S. government a clear picture of the applicant’s proposed mission parameters, and is intended to satisfy aspects of the licensing requirements for other space-regulating agencies.” OSC intends to continue to develop the application to certify different types of in-space activities like in-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing; orbital data centers; and lunar surface activity. OSC will take public comment on the process as well. “I am excited to see the tremendous interest from our American space industry to help shape this process with their participation and collaboration. We are ready to get their innovative capabilities to ‘yes,’” commented Taylor Jordan, Assistant Secretary of Commerce and Director of the Office of Space Commerce. candidates.title: Live Coverage: Starship Flight 15 attempts to recover full vehicle in double launch pad catch
candidates.raw_excerpt: The fully stacked Starship Flight 15 vehicle stands ready for launch from Starbase, Texas. Image: Adam Bernstein/Spaceflight Now. SpaceX is gearing up for its most ambitious Starship flight to date, hoping to demonstrate its revolutionary rocket is fully reusable by recovering both its first and second stages. And like on the previous mission, Starship Flight 15 will deploy 26 Starlink Version 3 satellites into orbit from its ‘Pez’ dispenser in the stainless steel belly of the ship. Liftoff of the integrated Starship vehicle from Starbase in Texas is scheduled during a 75-minute launch window that opens at 4:45 p.m. CST (5:45 p.m. EST / 2245 UTC) on Friday, Nov. 13. Spaceflight Now will have live coverage starting about 90 minutes prior to launch. SpaceX’s flight plan calls for Super Heavy Booster 22 to return to pad 2 at Starbase about 6.5 minutes after launching from there. It will be caught by the launch tower’s robotic arms, known as the ‘chopsticks’. If all goes according to plan, it will mark the first time a Version 3 Super Heavy Booster has returned to the pad. Three previous boosters were caught by the launch pad tower. If Ship 42 vehicle successfully reaches orbit and SpaceX mission control deems it healthy, it will remain in space for up to 14 orbits of the planet, before making its own return to the launch site, 22.5 hours after launch or at around 3:17 p.m. CST (4:17 p.m. EST / 2117 UTC). SpaceX has options to end the mission early with splashdowns off Hawaii and Chile if there is any doubt about the safety of a landing attempt at Starbase, which will take the craft over Mexico and South Texas. If both stages return successfully, it would be the first full recovery of an orbital launch system. SpaceX said on its website that would be “a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket.”

candidates.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
candidates.raw_excerpt: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up. But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes. What's happening and when to look You can easily see the Pleiades as a bright misty patch in your peripheral vision during winter. (Image credit: Haitong Yu via Getty Images) The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns. In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. While technically not dead, bleached coral is more susceptible disease — and a harbinger to demise from starvation. It’s a breakthrough that could potentially be used to save countless reefs from succumbing to climate change. Almost ten percent of the world’s reefs have been lost over the last 30 years, and bleaching events are only getting more severe as the effects of rising temperatures worsen. It took just seven weeks for the former to recover, while the latter succumbed to starvation. candidates.title: Astronomers trace mystery radio signals back to cosmic odd couple of white dwarf and sun-like star
candidates.raw_excerpt: Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star. The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153. GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs. The unusual system consists of a small and highly energetic white dwarf pulsar, orbiting a much larger star similar to our sun. (Image credit: ICRAR) "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement . "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself." The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star. The timing of the personnel change is striking given that Trump first joined Kalshi as an advisor shortly before the November 2024 election. Now, his departure comes as tech leaders and their companies move to distance themselves from right-wing politics and the second Trump Administration ahead of Democrats taking back Congressional power in 2027 — with a broad mandate from voters to crack down on government corruption. He’s held advisor roles with both companies, and as Bloomberg notes, he received hundreds of thousands of dollars in equity from Kalshi in exchange for his work. A Kalshi spokesperson told Bloomberg that the decision to part ways was due to Trump Jr.’s investment in its rival, which wasn’t at all a secret that would suddenly be an issue post-midterm. “We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer,” said the company. “We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers.” Democrats have vowed to launch investigations into corruption once in power, and should they follow through, the Trump family’s relationships with Kalshi and Polymarket will certainly come under Congressional scrutiny. candidates.title: I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review
candidates.raw_excerpt: Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope. Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit. At 25 lbs (11.33 kg), the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a relative heavyweight. Jamie Carter The supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces provide 30x and 75x magnification, respectively, but are obvious candidates for future upgrades. Jamie Carter The StarSense Explorer smartphone dock uses a small mirror. Jamie Carter It was a stunning view, and exactly the kind of experience a beginner needs from a first telescope. There was no frustration and no wondering whether I was looking in the right place. StarSense took me straight there — but, crucially, I moved the telescope myself. I’ve always liked that combination of hand-holding and DIY observing that Celestron’s StarSense tech gives you. I’m less convinced by the tabletop telescope it’s attached to. Although this $599 RRP (£379) model is significantly smaller than the Celestron StarSense Explorer 8-inch Dobsonian telescope I’ve previously reviewed, it still weighs 25 lbs (11.33 kg). You need to place it on something sturdy before you can use it comfortably. After living with it in my backyard, I’m not convinced the tabletop format is the advantage it initially appears to be. What is it? On Wednesday, New York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers. The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military. This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event. Why is it incredible? Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025 . She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017. One prominent example is Hu Anming, a Chinese-Canadian laser physicist who was fired from his research position at the University of Tennessee Knoxville in 2020 after groundless allegations surfaced that he was engaged in economic espionage on behalf of the Chinese government. candidates.raw_excerpt: Three Canadian companies are racing Moon-cart concepts. Canadensys, MDA Space, and Mission Control collectively received C$14.6M ($10.3M) in July 2025 for a Phase 0 lunar-utility-rover study supporting Artemis. And now, work is almost done. Phase shift: This year, NASA unveiled its plan to build a Moon Base —an undertaking that will require a transportation network that includes big rovers. As a result, CSA is expected to boost funding for its rover projects, and a new RFP should drop within days that will downselect to two companies to keep building in 2027 alongside science-instrument procurements. MDA Space is a competitor in the rover procurement, as well as the maker of Canadarm3—originally intended to be used for Gateway. A company official told Payload that lunar mobility will enhance Moon Base support alongside possibly repurposed robotics, under examination through a funded task authorization with CSA. Moon Meccano: CSA is asking industry to design a fully robotic rover, roughly the size of two pickup trucks side by side, that must fit on a 1.5m-by-1m pallet. Mid-design phase, CSA chose to shelve designs for the four-ton rover initially envisioned for 2034—at least temporarily—and asked companies to instead target a two-ton product that could ship ~3 to ~4 years faster. Given the Moon Base timeline, waiting until 2034 risked the tech becoming “obsolete,” Mission Control CEO and founder Ewan Reid told Payload. “As a collective industry, an ecosystem in Canada, I think we all looked at ourselves and recognized that,” added Reid, whose company has developed tech, instruments, and software for several Moon missions already. The companies emphasized the rover tech has applications for other Moon projects, even if their concept isn’t selected. “We’re actively part of rover programs for the US, and for the European Space Agency as well,” Canadensys President and CEO Christian Sallaberger told Payload. Tanzania plans to generate 1,892 megawatts (MW) of electricity from renewable energy sources by 2030 as part of efforts to boost the country's total power generation capacity to 8,000 MW, a senior government official said on Thursday.

James Mataragio, permanent secretary in the Ministry of Energy responsible for petroleum and gas, made the remarks at the opening of the 2026 Renewable Energy Week conference in Dar es Salaam.

Mataragio said renewable energy sources, including solar, wind and biomass, would play a significant role in achieving the national electricity generation target.

He noted that the country's Development Vision 2050 aims to increase electricity generation capacity to 70 gigawatts by 2050.

Achieving these ambitious targets would require substantial investment, innovative technologies and strategic partnerships among the government, the private sector and development partners, he added.

Tanzania currently has an installed electricity generation capacity of 4,667 MW from various sources, including hydropower, natural gas, biomass, solar, coal and wind, he said.

The government is also implementing its 2024–2034 National Clean Cooking Energy Strategy, which aims to ensure that 80% of Tanzanians have access to clean cooking energy by 2034, while the National Energy Compact targets 75% by 2030, he said.

candidates.raw_excerpt:
Microsoft's latest failure was global in reach, but not global in impact.

From around 4.17 p.m. UTC on Thursday, the US tech giant's services including Outlook, Teams, Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot, were degraded for more than 10 hours. The disruption reached at least 74 countries, with Outlook complaints on Downdetector – a third-party outage-monitoring platform that aggregates user reports – peaking near 140,000. 

The damage was heavily concentrated in the Americas, Europe and Australia. Governments didn't treat it as a purely private-sector issue. Germany's federal cybersecurity authority, BSI, said it was in contact with Microsoft and that "numerous companies" had been cut off from core cloud services. Australia's Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said he had activated a mechanism requiring Microsoft to prioritize the country's recovery, after both the Australian Federal Police and the domestic intelligence agency ASIO confirmed they were hit. Japan's government said its shared administrative IT backbone, GSS, was disrupted forcing some ministries back to phone communication. The Philippines' Supreme Court warned that email responses and online transactions would be delayed.

China sat in a blank space on that map. 

Why China was unfazed 

Multinationals in Shanghai on Microsoft's global platform were hit, as were Chinese exporters whose partners live on Outlook. Some foreign firms and foreign-related personnel in China using the global version were still affected. But the broader country didn't blink.

candidates.title: Starship Flight 15: Booster diverts to ocean, but Ship 42 makes history
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX has caught a Starship upper stage for the first time. After 22 and a half hours and 14 orbits, Ship 42 returned over land to Starbase on Saturday and was caught by the chopsticks at Pad 2 . Flight 15/Starlink Group 31-2 set out to catch both stages of an orbital-class rocket, something no one in spaceflight history has done. Booster 22 aborted its own return shortly after launch on Friday and diverted to the Gulf, but Ship 42 completed its return over land for the first ship catch. Ship 42 Caught Ship 42 lifted off with Booster 22 at around 4:47 pm CST on Nov. 13. It deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, then coasted for more than 20 hours while flight controllers monitored its systems. After passing the final return check, the ship performed a good deorbit burn on a single sea-level Raptor and reentered, crossing Mexico on its way back to South Texas. It flew a final swoosh maneuver out over the Gulf, then broke through the clouds and lit three Raptors for the landing flip. The chopsticks closed around the ship at around 3:21 pm CST on Nov. 14. THEY CAUGHT A SHIP! Starship Flight 15: Ship 42 returns to launch site! https://t.co/hEwe4Lwmim pic.twitter.com/4nuNluG1zU — NSF – NASASpaceflight.com (@NASASpaceflight) November 14, 2026 Within about 20 minutes, teams had positioned the ship on the chopsticks and attached the Ship Quick Disconnect (SQD). Ship 42’s heat shield appeared to be in good condition after reentry. Booster 22 Divert Booster 22 relit 32 of its planned 33 Raptors for boostback, but the burn ended early due to low fuel mass. SpaceX says the root cause is under investigation. The booster’s guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) system triggered an automated abort during coast and diverted it to an offshore landing location. It performed a landing burn while hovering over the Gulf, and its flight termination system was triggered when the engines shut down. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days. "For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville said in a statement .
