Thanks to Chandra ’s X-ray vision, Aghakhanloo has led a team of astronomers who think they have now uncovered an explanation. How did a cosmic vampire hide as a supernova? These are the most massive and luminous stars in the universe and their extreme characteristics result in them being highly unstable, undergoing intermittent bouts of mass loss as they eject material from their outer layers into the surrounding space. However, faking a supernova is not part of their typical behavior, so a new way of looking at AT 2016blu was needed. candidates.raw_excerpt: It’s undeniable that Elon Musk has radically shaken up the satellite industry. With thousands of satellites launched and thousands more planned, Starlink has managed to position itself as the dominant force in satellite connectivity. However, beneath the surface lies an important question for satellite network operators (SNOs), mobile network operators (MNOs), governments, and the wider space industry: Is the Starlink model truly the most efficient, cost-effective, and sustainable approach to global connectivity? Starlink’s constellation strategy is to blanket the planet with coverage using Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites. But this brute-force approach, while impressive, comes with critical disadvantages that the industry can no longer afford to ignore. Operators should instead consider an alternative approach, focusing on smarter, regionally focused constellations that deliver targeted, fixed broadband coverage with significantly fewer satellites, substantially lower capital expenditure, and much greater sustainability. The Fill-Rate Fallacy A disadvantage of the Starlink approach-and other large LEO constellations is the low utilization or “fill rate” of satellites. Our analysis suggests Starlink’s global coverage model leads to a fill rate of around 8% to 10%. This is unsurprising given that about 71% of Earth’s surface is covered by water, and only 1% consists of densely populated urban areas where broadband demand is highest. More than 90% of these satellites spend most of their operational lives over oceans and remote, unpopulated areas, representing inherent inefficiency. To put this into perspective, the next generation Starlink V3 satellite weighs about two tons and will alone provide more than 1 Tbps of throughput. candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement. The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired. When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down. Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet. The European Space Agency's Rosetta spacecraft captured these photos of the Philae lander descending toward, and then bouncing off, the surface of Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko during its historic touchdown on Nov. 12, 2014. (Image credit: ESA/Rosetta/MPS for OSIRIS Team MPS/UPD/LAM/IAA/SSO/INTA/UPM/DASP/IDA) Why it mattered The European Space Agency 's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of. The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P , all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned. After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. candidates.raw_excerpt: We've had no shortage of great Warhammer 40K games lately, but most aren't exactly aimed at the casual crowd. Warhammer Survivors changes that, finally providing curious gamers with an easy entry point into the grim darkness of the 41st millennium. Developed by Auroch Digital (in collaboration with Vampire Survivors' Poncle), this new spin on the survivors-like roguelite subgenre mixes the sci-fi 40,000 setting with the pure fantasy Age of Sigmar universe. This means heroes and enemies from all over the Warhammer mythos meet together in a bite-sized game that anyone can figure out and enjoy in less than five minutes. When you look at the alternatives, that's a remarkable achievement for a franchise that's notoriously hard (and often expensive) to get into . Warhammer Survivors isn't bogged down by dense lore, involved mechanics, or massive campaign playthroughs. It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun 's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos. All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula. If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. You battle an endless onslaught of enemies that slowly march towards you, with your character passively attacking automatically. You only need to move them around sprawling arenas and select level-up upgrades and items after collecting enough gems (skulls in this case). candidates.title: I used the Vaonis Vespera 3 for weeks and here’s who I would recommend it to — full review
candidates.raw_excerpt: I’ve spent a lot of time with smart telescopes , from relatively inexpensive Seestar models to the original Vaonis Vespera and the Vespera Pro . They all promise essentially the same thing — you put a telescope outside at night, choose something interesting on your smartphone and let the technology take care of the rest. The Vaonis Vespera 3 does that exceptionally well, but after spending several nights with it, I’m convinced it’s designed for a rather different kind of buyer. The telescope’s optical arm folds into its curved body when switched off. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) At $2,490/£2,199, this is hardly an impulse purchase for the beginner who’s curious about astronomy – you could buy several perfectly capable smart telescopes for the same money. Yet I found myself increasingly impressed by what the Vespera 3 could achieve, particularly when I returned to the same object over several nights. The images were sharp, the colors were excellent and I almost never had to think about the battery. The Vespera III weighs 13 lbs (6 kg) including the tripod. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) That doesn’t mean the experience was flawless. I sometimes spent longer than I’d have liked waiting for the telescope to get ready, but once it began photographing the sky, the Vespera 3 reminded me why I love smart telescopes so much. What begins as a fairly ordinary patch of stars gradually becomes something much more interesting. First a faint cloud of gas appears, then more structure emerges, and eventually you have an image that, only a few short years ago, would have been difficult to capture without specialist equipment. candidates.title: Satellite snaps rare birds-eye view of the ISS | Space photo of the day for Nov. 12, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: A satellite looks down at the International Space Station in orbit. (Image credit: HEO) A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above. What is it? Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments. But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory. HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range. This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO . So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024). Why is it incredible? While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface. A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.

After all, the path of totality crosses Luxor, home to Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the ancient world's most famous monuments. But follow the moon 's shadow west and another ancient civilization comes into view. Before reaching Egypt, totality will sweep across the Mediterranean and North Africa, passing over an extraordinary collection of Roman cities, fortresses, theaters, temples and triumphal arches. Many lie within what became Rome's North African provinces, a region that produced some of the empire's wealthiest and most impressive cities. From beachside Baelo Claudia in Spain and military Tamuda in Morocco to Timgad and Djémila in Algeria and the jaw-dropping El Jem Amphitheater in Tunisia, Roman ruins will experience between two and more than five minutes of darkness — creating extraordinary possibilities for eclipse chasers and photographers. candidates.title: SoftBank Loses $7 Billion as AI Data Centers Turn Out to Be Risky Investment
candidates.raw_excerpt: The AI data center boom is looking as shaky as ever. Nowhere is that more apparent than at the Japanese megafirm SoftBank — perhaps best known for bankrolling WeWork before its spectacular implosion — and which now seems to be standing on a financial snowpack that could collapse into an avalanche. SoftBank backstopped OpenAI , the lab behind ChatGPT, with over $60 billion in risky debt financing. As the Financial Times reports , that move has now dragged the bank into an ominous loss of $7 billion between July and September, the company’s first quarterly loss in two years of business. According to the FT , at least $3.7 billion of the loss is likely attributable to a massive OpenAI data center development in Ohio. SoftBank initially blamed that portion on financing for “existing and planned” data center projects there, before backtracking to say the losses are “completely unrelated” to any dealings in the buckeye state. Compare SoftBank’s $7 billion overall drop to its profit of $2.17 billion the previous quarter, or its heady $15.64 billion profit over the third quarter of 2025, and it’s clear the firm is currently hemorrhaging money to keep some AI dreams alive. Shares in the company have also plummeted by nearly 50 percent since June, the FT notes, as ratings downgrades and rising skepticism over the viability of the AI industry scare investors into safer corners of the market. In order to keep pumping money into AI powerlabs like OpenAI, SoftBank itself has started digging into junk bonds — high-risk debt, essentially — raising over $11 billion in non-investment grade bonds in September. So on top of boasting perhaps one of the highest degrees of exposure to the AI bubble on the planet, the Japanese investment firm is now the world-record holder for the largest corporate junk bond offering ever made. With a foundation this unstable, it’s no wonder SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son calls the AI bubble a myth — because if it exists, his megabank is in mega trouble.

candidates.title: Astronomers stunned after James Webb Space Telescope discovers the earliest pair of black hole-powered quasars
candidates.raw_excerpt: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have discovered the oldest pair of supermassive black hole-powered quasars ever seen. There's just one problem: they shouldn't exist! The compact quasar pair, spotted with the aid of the Gemini North telescope, has been designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, which means "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the universe." The compact quasar pair is seen as it was 900 million years after the Big Bang at a time when such supermassive black holes should not have had time to grow to such tremendous masses. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua isn't just the oldest and most distant quasar pairing ever seen. There is just 18,100 light-years, or roughly one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way, between the supermassive black holes, which have masses of 1.5 billion and 400 million times that of the sun. That makes Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua the most compact quasar pair found during a period of the universe's history known as Cosmic Dawn , shortly after the birth of the first stars, galaxies, and black holes. "There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two," research team leader Silvia Onorato of the NOIRLab said in a statement . "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the universe was only a thirteenth of its age and, astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today." How were supermassive black holes over fed at Cosmic Dawn Quasars occur when the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of large galaxies are surrounded by a flattened cloud of swirling gas and dust called an "accretion disk," from which they feed or "accrete" matter. candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627. Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-627 mission for the U.S. Space Force from California on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated , however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world. SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth . In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean. It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103. A Falcon 9 first stage rests on a SpaceX drone ship shortly after launching the USSF-627 mission on Nov. 11, 2026. candidates.title: As Multiple Affairs Emerge, Calls Grow for Jensen Huang to Resign
candidates.raw_excerpt: As more information comes out about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s numerous affairs with high-profile figures in the tech world, calls are mounting for the embattled chief to resign from his post. So far, numerous members of congress from both sides of the aisle have been joined by media figures like Fox Business host Larry Kudlow in calling for Huang to step down from what is arguably one of the most powerful posts in the world right now. Publications like the Economist have also issued blistering editorials calling for his resignation, characterizing Huang as a “brilliant man — and a fool.” The snafu all stems from reporting by the Financial Times , which recently unveiled that one of Huang’s affairs was with the executive of a Singaporean AI company named Alice Huang. Per the FT ’s reporting, anonymous sources in the US intelligence community believe the woman is a spy for the Chinese government — claims that sparked a massive debate around Nvidia’s central position in the world economy. Setting aside the putrid ethics of cheating on your spouse , whether Huang’s mistress was really a Chinese operative remains to be seen. For starters, the evidence traces back to anonymous US intelligence agents, the kind who have been known to sensationalize when it comes to tales of Chinese spies in high places (China firmly denied the accusation, dismissing it as a smear tactic by the West.) Beyond Huang, this wouldn’t be the first time the AI industry has had a freakout about seductive honeys from foreign lands, a tacitly xenophobic narrative drawn from Cold War pulp novels. And from another point of view, Huang’s ousting may come at the perfect time. Financial markets are experiencing turmoil as fears around a hyperinflated AI bubble become mainstream . If someone in Huang’s position was ever going to get out while the getting is good, it seems now would be the time — though given how topsy-turvy this saga has been already, what the AI chip billionaire does next is anyone’s guess

candidates.raw_excerpt: A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG). Here's the PSRA strategy: Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth Assess proposed mission requirements Review prior lessons learned Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028. Pick-me-ups The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples. NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars , as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself. Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet. NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment. candidates.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
candidates.raw_excerpt: Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources. As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now. "Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them. The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 11, 1966: NASA launches Gemini 12 mission with astronaut icons Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell aboard
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks. Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day. The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program . Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 , and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13 . The Gemini 12 astronauts James Lovell and Edwin Aldrin lifted off aboard a Titan launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center on November 11, 1966, an hour and a half after their Agena target vehicle was orbited by an Atlas rocket. (Image credit: NASA/MSFC) Why it mattered Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon. It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11. candidates.title: Andy Weir's 'Exoplanet' just landed on Audible, but what actually makes an exoplanet habitable?
candidates.raw_excerpt: Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. candidates.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
candidates.raw_excerpt: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. candidates.title: Astronomers Puzzled After Watching Entire Planet Wink Out of Sight
candidates.raw_excerpt: An international team of astronomers were puzzled when an entire gas giant appeared to vanish from the sky. The disappearing exoplanet, dubbed TOI-2535 b, is located roughly 1,000 light-years from Earth. Since it orbits its host star at an extremely close distance, completing a full rotation in just over eight days, its surface is extremely hot, making it a “hot Jupiter.” NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the planet numerous times between 2019 and 2026. But there was something strange afoot: its brightness progressively dipped every time it passed in front of its star, and it also had a tendency to show up far too early or too late. And then, in a cosmic vanishing act, it failed to show up at all this year. In a new article published in the Astrophysical Journal Letters journal, an international team of scientists dug into the mystery. And they’ve cooked up an explanation for the “disappearing act,” suggesting that a still-unobserved neighboring planet could be messing with TOI-2535 b’s orbit significantly. According to their calculations, the “two planets make each other’s orbits wobble like a top,” causing them to disappear from view as they come out of alignment. That kind of chaotic arrangement is par for the course in an unpredictable universe filled with oddball star systems. “We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” University of California, Los Angeles postdoctoral fellow and corresponding author on the paper Samuel Yee said in a statement . “If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits. We know of a few systems that are like this.” “This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly,” he added. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.” TOI-2535 b is one of several hundred hot Jupiters that have been discovered to date. candidates.title: Hubble Space Telescope reveals glittering stars with mysterious origins | Space photo of the day for Nov. 11, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange. But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed. M30 is a globular star cluster located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth. (Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini) What is it? The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus. M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity . Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old! Why is it amazing Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell. Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history. Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Donald Trump’s social media platform Truth Social is cratering right along with his personal reputation, but it does have one thing going for it: customers dumb enough to pay top dollar for slightly faster access to the president’s posts — or “truths,” in the site’s oxymoronic nomenclature. The gains primarily came from its so-called “Truth API,” a feed that gives early access to posts by certain accounts — and let’s be real, people are paying for Trump’s — for the price of between $60,000 and $100,000 per month . The feed was blasted as being an obvious rip-off the moment it was announced, and a blatant attempt to cash in on the president’s potentially consequential ramblings. candidates.title: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
candidates.raw_excerpt: A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum. UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) . The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement . "The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement. candidates.title: Isaacman lays out SLS path to the 2030s
candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has further explained the decision to standardize the Space Launch System (SLS), move toward a stretched Centaur V upper stage, and stop work on Mobile Launcher 2 (ML-2), linking those choices to higher flight rates and lower costs. Speaking on NSF’s The Flame Trench show, Isaacman said industry’s responses to NASA’s search for future commercial lunar transportation pointed to the 2030s, rather than an immediate replacement for the existing system. His explanation built on NASA’s previously announced decision to abandon SLS Block 1B and its Exploration Upper Stage (EUS) . The emphasis was on improving the hardware and operations available now while preparing for a later transition. “There are a lot of ways to shake the $4 billion disposable rocket label that SLS has carried and one of which is launch more frequently,” Isaacman said. “There is nothing about pushing it off into next year that makes anything cost less,” he added. Centaur V and a standardized SLS Artemis IV was previously intended to introduce Block 1B and EUS. NASA instead moved toward a near-Block 1 configuration using Centaur V, avoiding continued development of an upper stage dedicated to SLS. Centaur V is already in production for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket . It first flew on Vulcan’s Cert-1 mission in January 2024 , while the broader Centaur family provides decades of flight heritage. However, the stretched version planned for NASA remains in development. Isaacman said NASA originally intended to use the existing Centaur configuration, but pursued the higher-performance version as part of efforts to move Orion closer to the Moon and simplify the landers’ task. The study’s abstract also points to a rising number of cases reported by healthcare professionals involving irregular heart rhythm or sudden cardiac death in otherwise healthy young adults who regularly slurp down energy drinks. Crucially, the findings point to a high number of adverse heart impacts in young adults in the 18-to-34 age range, for whom heart conditions are generally rare. candidates.raw_excerpt: There’s something puzzling about 1998 KY26, a mysterious object that the Japanese space agency’s Hayabusa2 spacecraft is on its way to visit: it’s accelerating. That isn’t necessarily out of the ordinary for asteroids and comets, but it appears to be driven by a propulsion source that scientists have yet to understand, as ScienceAlert reports . One explanation, from Harvard astronomer Avi Loeb, suggests that 1998 KY26 is a derelict Soviet spacecraft that launched almost 40 years ago. More conventional attempts to account for its acceleration proffer that it’s a “dark comet,” a type of space object that acts like a rocky asteroid, but experiences acceleration that can’t be accounted for by gravitational forces. Yet according to new research published in the journal Icarus , it’s too warm to be a dark comet, which can accelerate by releasing ice that sublimates into gas. If that were the case, observations show that it would’ve run out of ice reserves a long time ago. “Our temperature model results indicate that the water outgassing rate on 1998 KY26 would be too high to maintain buried ice, refining the understanding of the asteroid’s composition,” authors of the paper and Georgia Institute of Technology aerospace engineers Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi wrote. 1998 KY26 is a 36-foot space object that rotates every five and a half minutes and is currently located 186 million miles away from Earth. After modeling its temperature using pre-existing data, Hansen and Hirabayashi found that even its coldest regions measured upwards of -77 degrees Fahrenheit. While that may sound chilly, it’s too warm for stores of ice that could sublimate into gas and provide thrust. At such warm temperatures, 1998 KY26 would’ve run out of fuel in just 62 years, a blink of an eye for an object suspected to be billions of years old, as ScienceAlert points out. candidates.raw_excerpt: NMFS proposes to amend regulations that prohibit commercial fishing in the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument Expansion (PRIMNM Expansion), which comprises waters of the U.S. exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between 50 to 200 nautical miles (nmi; 93 to 370 kilometers (km)) around Johnston Atoll and Wake and Jarvis Islands. This action is necessary to conform fishing regulations with Presidential Proclamation 10918 of April 17, 2025--Unleashing American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific, as amended by Presidential Proclamation 11035 of June 11, 2026--Restoring American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific, and in light of a court order. Fisheries in the PRIMNM Expansion would be regulated pursuant to existing fishing regulations under the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act), the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Convention Implementation Act (WCPFCIA), the South Pacific Tuna Act (SPTA), and other applicable laws, that apply to all U.S. commercial fishing vessels but were superseded and made inapplicable when the commercial fishing prohibition for the PRIMNM Expansion was established. The proposed rule supports the long-term sustainability of U.S. fisheries and provides for the proper care and management of the PRIMNM and PRIMNM Expansion and the objects of historic or scientific interest therein, as directed by Proclamation 10918, as amended by Proclamation 11035.

candidates.title: Trump Admin Caught Illegally Canceling Billion-Dollar Solar Project That Would Have Helped Lower Utility Bills Across the Country
candidates.raw_excerpt: Donald Trump and his Republican lackeys were decimated in this week’s midterm elections , in large part thanks to an ongoing cost of living crisis. While there are many factors making life hard on Americans financially, one of the key stressors is the cost of energy, which has skyrocketed in the wake of the tech industry’s data center buildout. Much of that pain could have been avoided — or at least pre-empted — had the Trump administration allowed a billion-dollar solar panel development project go ahead as planned, Boston-area public radio station WBUR reported . According to the broadcaster’s reporting, the Environmental Protection Agency under Trump appointee Lee Zeldin has refused to dish out billions of congressionally-approved funds meant to expand access to solar energy in low-income communities. The Biden-era program, dubbed “Solar For All,” earmarked $7 billion for distribution to solar energy developments led by states and Tribal governments. States like Massachusetts and Michigan were previously approved for $156 million, while others like Arkansas were set to receive over $93 million. But when it came time for the federal government to pay the piper, Zeldin and the EPA refused , calling it a “boondoggle.” That decision set off an immediate legal battle, which was recently resolved in favor of the Solar For All recipients. Despite a federal court order that the government dish out the funds, the EPA has yet to loosen its purse strings, leaving questions as to whether the agency will appeal the decision — or even ignore it entirely. “This is a program that has the potential to lower people’s energy bills, get inexpensive clean electricity on the grid, and help the communities that the Solar For All program was designed to help,” senior attorney at the Conservation Law Foundation James Crowley, who is representing plaintiffs in one of the court cases, told WBUR . candidates.title: Microsoft AI CEO Says He’s Open to Agents Deserving Rights If He Sees the Right Evidence
candidates.raw_excerpt: Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft’s AI CEO — a human in charge of its AI operations, we should clarify — says he’s willing to consider giving AI models rights if they ever become conscious. But he really doesn’t want that to happen in the first place. The comments came in a post he made on X clarifying some of the things he said in a recent essay he penned on “model welfare.” He began that essay with an unequivocal statement: “AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer.” That shouldn’t be too controversial. But in this day and age, when trillion dollar AI companies like Anthropic are pushing the idea that their language models could already be conscious, it very much is . This was not lost on Suleyman, who observed in his update that a “surprising number of people on X think we should take AI rights seriously.” As such, Suleyman clarified that he doesn’t think that “AIs cannot be conscious.” What he meant is that they aren’t currently — and, if he had his way, “this is how they must remain.” Reading comprehension is apparently hard for the model welfare crowd, since Suleyman’s original remarks already seemed pretty clear about the tense he was discussing. But he took the opportunity to elaborate on his positions further, saying that while he has seen “no evidence that AIs are conscious or deserve welfare,” he would update his position if “that data emerges.” It’s perhaps lending too much credence to the idea of AI consciousness, since any evidence that the current architecture of AI models is even capable of supporting something like human experience remains incredibly controversial. But the debate is dominated by sci-fi primed paranoia. However far-fetched certain ideas about AI may seem, they have large contingents in the AI industry taking them seriously . candidates.title: Climate Change Has Become So Bad That Rice Krispies Don’t Have Actual Rice in Them Anymore
candidates.raw_excerpt: Snap, Crackle, and Pop! The sonic slogan of Rice Krispies is now becoming an anachronism. The classic puffed rice foodstuff now no longer contain actual rice grains, at least in UK and European markets, the manufacturer Kellogg’s recently admitted . It will now use rice flour and corn flour, which aside from gustatory concerns, will result in it being noticeably quieter than it used to be. Kellogg’s, in the face of complaints online, insists that retaining the original sound was a “huge focus.” It’s yet another example of the corporate cost-cutting putrefaction we’ve come to expect — and the reason for it is grim: climate change. A spokesperson told media outlets that the reformulation will help “maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals.” The company didn’t get into specifics, but the recipe change comes as a powerful “ super El Niño ” climate phenomenon has devastated agriculture in South and Southeast Asia , where more than half the world’s rice is grown. Scientists say that the impacts of the weather event, which is on track to be the most powerful of its kind in recorded history, has been exacerbated by climate change. The “changing weather patterns” referred to by the Kellogg’s spokesperson was an understatement. El Niño is characterized by warming ocean surface temperatures in the Pacific. This kicks off a chain reaction that causes formidable storms and rainfall in the Americas while severely disrupting rainfall patterns and bringing devastating droughts across Asia. Asian rice prices have climbed to their highest in almost two years as El Niño has impacted rice production, Bloomberg reported , while the US Department of Agriculture is forecasting a decline in global rice production for the first time in over a decade. In the grand scheme of things, a cereal reformulation sounds like a trivial casualty in the face of an unfolding climate
